power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Mathematical Relationships Between Brains and Consciousness

author.affiliation:

text.text: A chief aim of the neuroscience of consciousness is to derive how states of conscious experience (i.e., qualia) are related to supporting brain states (e.g., patterns of neural activation within patterns of neural connectivity).
This aim goes beyond identifying neuronal correlates of consciousness (NCC) on the one side, and beyond structural descriptions of conscious experience (e.g., qualia structure) on the other side.
The ultimate goal is to link these two sides by mapping specific neuronal states or mechanisms to specific conscious experiences.
Relating two or more phenomena in science often takes the form of mathematical mappings, such as equations (e.g., E = mc^2).
This raises the possibility that there also are mathematical mappings that relate conscious states to brain states.
Here we review empirical work on mapping neuronal spiking activity to conscious contents.

We specifically discuss pioneering paradigms aimed at identifying "bridge loci", in the form of NCC, and paradigms aimed at identifying "bridge laws", such as relating psychometric to neurometric functions.
We then examine how these paradigms are augmented by mapping structural descriptions of conscious experience to structural descriptions of neuronal activity.
One of the central ideas of the Qualia-Structure Project is to mathematically relate structural descriptions of brain mechanisms to structural descriptions of conscious experience (qualia).
In the following, we will discuss prior, mostly non-structural, attempts at mathematically relating brain mechanisms to conscious experience.
We do so in order to provide greater historical and empirical context.
This includes known mathematical relations between brain mechanisms and qualia as well as successes and limitations of non-structural mathematical approaches.
This contextual knowledge is vital to fully appreciate the rationale and motivation as well as historical development of various approaches and methods utilized by the Qualia Structure Project.
Humans have long wondered how consciousness relates to our physical bodies, or brains.
This question is called the mind-body problem (Van Gulick 2004) https://paperpile.com/c/nGV3XJ/dF25x or in modern terms, the mind-brain problem.
text.formatted: This question is called the mind-body problem <ref type="bibr" target="#b175">(Van Gulick 2004)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/nGV3XJ/dF25x">,</ref> or in modern terms, the mind-brain problem.

text.text: There is much at stake.
If the existence of our conscious experience depends on the existence of our brains, our consciousness will cease to exist once our brains cease to exist.
On the flip side, consciousness after death seems of greater likelihood if consciousness does not depend on intact brains.
These logical consequences of seemingly empirical questions are rarely discussed within scientific contexts.

And perhaps as a consequence, a significant fraction of neuroscientists are at risk of holding two or more opposing philosophical beliefs about the mind-brain problem at once (Navarro-Peña et al. 2026 https://paperpile.com/c/nGV3XJ/h3mn.

text.text: Yet, one has to admit that despite millennia of study, the relationship between our bodies (brains) and our conscious experience remains largely enigmatic (Chalmers 2010; Levine 1983).
text.formatted: Yet, one has to admit that despite millennia of study, the relationship between our bodies (brains) and our conscious experience remains largely enigmatic <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Chalmers 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Levine 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Some people react to the state of ignorance outlined above by assuming that only philosophy or theology can provide satisfying answers.
Given that there is no agreed-upon scientific explanation for how brains link to consciousness, this possibility cannot be ruled out.
Yet, many questions once deemed exclusive to philosophy or theology, such as whether the universe has always existed, are now addressed by science (Smeenk and Ellis 2017).
text.formatted: Yet, many questions once deemed exclusive to philosophy or theology, such as whether the universe has always existed, are now addressed by science <ref type="bibr" target="#b157">(Smeenk and Ellis 2017)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, the fact that science established the Big Bang theory, did not eliminate philosophical and theological debates on why and how our universe came into being.
We may find ourselves in a similar situation when it comes to the mind-body problem.
Indeed, there are several concrete questions that place the mind-brain problem squarely within (neuro)science (Crick and Koch 1995 , 1992 , 1998).

text.text: Consider that we do not currently have a complete scientific account for why or how general anesthesia causes loss of consciousness (Brown et al. 2010; Moody et al. 2021; Mashour and Alkire 2013).

text.text: We also have learned that some patients who get diagnosed as comatose are conscious, yet are unable to respond (Owen et al. 2006; Owen 2019; Owen et al. 2007).

text.text: Here, too, we have no reliable scientific way to detect consciousness when behavioral responses are not available.

The potential of detecting conscious experience via brain mechanisms (i.e., neuronal activity embedded in connectivity, or how neuronal states affect subsequent neural states) provides hope that we can help people in these undesirable scenarios.
The problem, then, is to find a reliable relationship between brain mechanisms and conscious experience, be it between levels of consciousness, contents of consciousness, or both.

There already are several promising approaches, but none of them have enjoyed universal success (e.g., (Massimini et al. 2009; Rosow and Manberg 2001; Maschke et al. 2023 Maschke et al. , 2024;; Nilsen et al. 2024; Yichun Gu et al. 2024)).
text.formatted: There already are several promising approaches, but none of them have enjoyed universal success (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(Massimini et al. 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">Rosow and Manberg 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Maschke et al. 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Maschke et al. , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Nilsen et al. 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Yichun Gu et al. 2024)</ref>).

text.text: Without first uncovering the relationship between brains and consciousness, remedies might remain elusive (after all, it is hard to fix a broken car without knowing how a car works in the first place).
The brain-consciousness relation, thus, is not just of intellectual interest.
It is a practical (neuroscientific) problem that demands a solution.
Having established that there is a relationship between brain mechanisms and conscious experience means that mathematical mappings between them are of interest.
In order to relate brain mechanisms to conscious states, it seems helpful to ensure that both sides of the link are using the same descriptors.

One way to accomplish this is to translate conscious states into mathematics since it is mathematics that is often used to describe brain mechanisms (see (Wigner 1960) and (Steiner 2009) for a deeper reflection on the role of mathematics in science).
text.formatted: One way to accomplish this is to translate conscious states into mathematics since it is mathematics that is often used to describe brain mechanisms (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b179">(Wigner 1960</ref>) and <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">(Steiner 2009</ref>) for a deeper reflection on the role of mathematics in science).

text.text: Once both conscious experience and brain mechanisms are described mathematically, it might be possible to derive mathematical mappings between these two descriptions.
This holds true even if a mathematical description of conscious experience (qualia) is deemed non-exhaustive.
That is, the mathematical mappings in question can be seen as purely methodological in nature (see (Ellia and Tsuchiya 2026) for discussion).
text.formatted: That is, the mathematical mappings in question can be seen as purely methodological in nature (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Ellia and Tsuchiya 2026</ref>) for discussion).

text.text: In fact, we already know of several mathematical mappings between (behaviorally indicated) conscious experiences and physical phenomena.
These mathematical laws have held up to decades of empirical research.
The existence of these laws calls into question the notion that there can be no mathematical mappings for conscious experience.
In the following, we will examine key historical developments in studying such mappings.
In particular, we will review the two main pioneering neuroscientific approaches that derived mathematical mappings between brain mechanisms and conscious experience.
This historical context explains both some of the origins and rationale of current Qualia Structure research as well as related structural approaches.
The early work reviewed here was largely limited to determining one or two-dimensional relations between brain mechanisms and conscious experience, such as coefficients or functions.

The Qualia Structure approach expands mathematical mappings between brains and conscious experience to much richer structures that can exceed two or three dimensions (though this is only one of many motivators for structural approaches; see (Tononi et al. 2025; Phillips and Tsuchiya 2024; Tsuchiya, Phillips, et al. 2022; Tsuchiya 2025; Fink and Lee 2026; Lee 2021; Kleiner 2024)).

text.text: After discussing the neuroscientific work that led up to the current structuralist approaches, we will briefly compare the chief differences between them.

We will stop short of an in-depth review of mappings between structural descriptions of conscious experience to structural descriptions of brain mechanisms, as we have already done so elsewhere (Maier and Tsuchiya 2026).

text.text: In the sections above, we made the case that (neuro-)science is justified in attempting to derive mappings between brain states and conscious states.
Somewhat surprisingly, this argument was not fully established, nor widely accepted, a few decades ago (Crick and Koch 1992 https://paperpile.com/c/nGV3XJ/QGxZ3.
text.formatted: Somewhat surprisingly, this argument was not fully established, nor widely accepted, a few decades ago <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Crick and Koch 1992</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://paperpile.com/c/nGV3XJ/QGxZ3">)</ref>.

text.text: As a consequence early studies often shied away from using the term "consciousness" and instead stuck to less contentious terms, such as "perception", or "awareness".

An added complication that afflicts both these pioneering studies as well as much ongoing research on the neuroscience of consciousness is the focus on studying the consciousness of others rather than one's own.
In practice, this "extrinsic" approach runs into at least two problems: (1) Measuring, and hence studying, behavior (such as verbal report or eye movements) rather than conscious experience directly.
(2) Limited knowledge about the presence of an experience and what that experience was like.
Notably, the scientific method does not prohibit the study of one's own experience (https://paperpile.com/c/nGV3XJ/DbR9.

text.text: In fact, the history of science provides ample precedence of single individuals performing experiments on themselves, including on their own experience (e.g., (Poldrack et al. 2015; Rivers and Head 1908; B. J. Marshall et al. 1985; McCance 1936)).

text.text: As we will discuss, there have been attempts of dropping reports (no-report paradigms), or enriching reports beyond simple yes/no responses (e.g., similarity ratings, micro-phenomenology).
However, as long as we study "other consciousness" rather than our own consciousness, the problem of "indirect" assessment remains.
There are benefits of studying "other consciousness", of course, such as that we can more easily find shared phenomena between individuals.

text.text: Whatever is required to elevate sensory brain responses to conscious experience may be subtle and thus might have to be studied in fine-grained detail.
Given the expectation that NCC might require fine-grained resolution, much of the earliest research centered on measurements of single neuron spiking activity.
Another benefit of this approach is that we know that neurons affect each other causally via spikes.

While we do not know whether it is spike-driven causality that provides the correct spatio-temporal grain for consciousness, spiking has been well established to be relevant to brain function in general, and many other potential grains (e.g., synaptic currents or the combined activity of cortical columns) are themselves in direct causal relation to spikes.

In contrast, most non-invasive (neuroimaging) techniques indirectly probe for spike-related activity, such as electromagnetic fields that penetrate the skull (EEG/MEG) or local changes in the brain's blood supply (fMRI).
The indirect nature of these techniques can pose interpretative challenges.

For example, repeated findings demonstrate that local fMRI responses can deviate from local spiking measurements (Epp et al. 2025; Maier et al. 2008; Sirotin and Das 2009; Chen et al. 2026; Rauscher et al. 2026).

text.text: One of the early approaches aimed at finding any relations between brain states and conscious states.
The focus was on isolating brain structures that correlate with conscious experience (neuronal correlates of consciousness, or NCC) to differentiate them from brain structures that do not.
The word "correlates" did not prescribe a mathematical procedure (such as correlation coefficients), but meant to indicate metaphysical noncommitment (i.e., to avoid notions of causality).

While NCC can be, and were, extended to neuronal mechanisms, such as neuronal synchrony, most NCC research stuck to identifying structures, such as neurons, areas, or networks whose activation coincided with certain contents of consciousness.
An impressive amount of literature has been amassed on the topic of "neuronal correlates of consciousness", though the rate of new papers has somewhat plateaued.

text.text: One reason for this approach is that it is largely theory-agnostic.
That is, rather than testing specific hypotheses about which brain mechanism leads to consciousness in a specific way, the idea was to first discover candidate subsets of brain mechanisms.
The most common type of paradigm used for this kind of analysis rests on a stimulus that is consciously experienced only some of the time (ideally, half of the time).
Above-threshold stimuli were more widely used than at-threshold stimuli (just-noticeable stimuli) that are so faint that they are only consciously perceived some of the time.

The reason for this preference is that conscious experience of at-threshold stimuli might be trivially explained by non-conscious factors such as spontaneous noise fluctuations at the receptor level, or fluctuating states of attention, arousal, or vigilance (https://paperpile.com/c/nGV3XJ/5MrYW.

text.text: Top: Physical stimulation (Retinal Input) is kept unchanging over time.
In the case of binocular rivalry, one image (e.g., a photograph of a face) is shown to one eye while a different image (e.g., a photograph of a house) is shown to the other eye.
When facing such conflict between the two eyes and if the stimuli are kept relatively small (1-2 degrees of visual angle), visual perception randomly alternates (switches) between each eye's view.

As a result, truthful subjects report that they either perceive one or the other image for brief periods of time (i.e., the Reported Percept alternates between the two mutually exclusive alternatives).

Middle: Some cortical neurons have been shown to either increase or decrease in firing rate whenever subjects report seeing one or the other image (i.e., researchers have found Single Neuron Activity that correlates with conscious perception).
Bottom left: Calculating the frequency of single neuron spiking during each of the two alternating perceptual states can be interpreted as two conditional probability distributions.
Bottom right: A statistical comparison of the mean or median spiking of a neuron to each of the two conscious perceptual states demonstrates significant differences in neuronal activation.

Any statistically significant difference in activation that occurs with alternating conscious experiences -despite constant retinal stimulation -is interpreted as a neuronal correlate of consciousness (NCC), suggesting that such a neuron's activity is associated with that conscious state.
Another aspect of early work on NCC was that it is largely focused on contents of consciousness rather than levels of consciousness such as dreamless sleep or coma.
And, in its most common form, the content of consciousness was reduced to a binary variable, such as "aware" and "unaware".
Given this reliance on contrasting two different states of consciousness, we will refer to the NCC approach as "state-based" (Figure 1).

text.text: The rationale was to "map bridge loci first (where?), then determine the bridge laws (how?)".
This logic rests on the assumption that NCC are static rather than dynamic.
If an NCC fluctuates across neurons rather than involving the same neurons, the task literally becomes a moving target.
Unfortunately, neurons sometimes are part of an NCC determined by the contrastive approach, and other times are not (Maier et al. 2007).

The gray labels of the two main clusters (NCC and Perceptual Decision Making) were added post hoc.
Note that the citation networks suggest two overlapping clusters in the early literature studying conscious visual perception.
One of these clusters was more heavily focused on mapping the activation of distinct neuronal structures, such as individual neurons or brain areas to conscious experience (NCC).
That is, these studies aimed to find "bridge loci" (where?) in the brain that could be linked to conscious experience.

The other cluster was more heavily focused on mapping mathematical (psychometric) functions that were derived from perceptual reports to mathematical (neurometric) functions that were derived from simultaneous recordings of neuronal activation.

That is, these studies aimed to derive "bridge laws" that formally describe (how?) neuronal activation supports conscious experience, though the actual mapping is to behavioral report (of "perception", and thus arguably conscious experience).
Around the same time, several groups used a somewhat different approach.

text.text: While the core of their research also exploited the fact that one and the same bistable physical stimulus sometimes evokes one conscious experience and sometimes another, these researchers did not just compare these two conditions in isolation.
Instead, they systematically (parametrically) varied the stimuli across trials to alter the likelihood of one conscious experience over another.
This results in a (psychometric) curve of reported occurrences for one percept (which arguably equates conscious experience) versus another as a function of stimulus manipulation.
These researchers then related these psychometric functions to a function of simultaneously collected single neuron spiking (neurometric functions).
Given this focus on mathematical functions, we will loosely group these studies as "function-based" mappings (Figure 3).

text.text: This literature is more commonly known as "perceptual decision making" (and the authors might object to being lumped into consciousness research).
"Decision making" was chosen to emphasize observable behavior (although the added word "perceptual" seemingly implies conscious experience as an inferred variable).

This approach does not just identify neurons that correlate with certain conscious experiences, but further provides a mathematical rule (bridge law) that links perceptual report to associated neuronal functions.
In practice, however, the single data point where a stimulus evoked each of two mutually exclusive conscious experiences with equal likelihood was used for analysis.

Using the neuronal responses to that stimulus, one can compute how much the responses of a neuron predict a certain conscious experience (i.e., a neuron's "choice probability" for a certain behavioral perceptual report).
There is a large body of literature on neuronal choice probability measures, with varying interpretations.

text.text: Subjects report which of two alternative perceptual states they experience.

A commonly used stimulus consists of randomly moving dots where the fraction (coherence) of dots moving in the same direction (e.g., left) is parametrically varied between stimulus presentations (trials).
On trials where the stimulus has zero coherence (not shown), subjects report that they see leftward motion about half of the time.
When experimenters increase the fraction (coherence) of dots moving to the left, subjects increasingly report that they perceive leftward motion.
When examined systematically, the result is a sigmoidal (s-shaped) curve called psychometric function, shown in blue.
A psychometric function describes the increased probability of a subject reporting "left" when presented with increasingly coherent stimuli.
At full 100% coherence, subjects report "left" with a probability close to 1.
Spiking activity that is simultaneously collected from a neuron can give rise to a similar sigmoidal function, called a neurometric function.

In this case, the s-shaped curve describes a statistic (d') of how well the neuron discriminates between the presented motion and a zero coherence stimulus (in practice, a stimulus of the same coherence, but opposite motion direction is often used).
There are various ways to mathematically compare the psychometric function to the neurometric function.

text.text: Perceptual similarity spaces form the basis for several techniques that we will discuss (i.e., representational similarity analyses and some of the more recent work of the Qualia Structure Project).
The basic idea of using space to represent similarity between individual perceptual objects, such as colors or auditory tones, goes back several decades (e.g., (Shepard 1982; Attneave 1950).
text.formatted: The basic idea of using space to represent similarity between individual perceptual objects, such as colors or auditory tones, goes back several decades (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b155">(Shepard 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Attneave 1950)</ref>.

text.text: As the name suggests, perceptual similarity spaces are established by asking subjects to rate the similarity between two sensory stimuli.
This numerical value then gets translated into a metric distance between them -the more similar, the less distance between them.
Using these pairwise distances, sensory stimuli then can be placed in a metric space, thus forming a structure.
Representational Similarity Analyses (RSA) can be used to map between similarity spaces (Kriegeskorte et al. 2008).
text.formatted: Representational Similarity Analyses (RSA) can be used to map between similarity spaces <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Kriegeskorte et al. 2008)</ref>.

text.text: RSA quantifies how much the pattern of pairwise distances is similar across two different similarity spaces.

In this context, the most interesting use of RSA is to map distances between the similarity of neuronal population responses to the distances between similarity ratings for the associated stimuli (Kriegeskorte 2009; Lin and Kriegeskorte 2024).
text.formatted: In this context, the most interesting use of RSA is to map distances between the similarity of neuronal population responses to the distances between similarity ratings for the associated stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Kriegeskorte 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Lin and Kriegeskorte 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, standard RSA usually quantifies pairwise dissimilarity distances rather than providing a full structure-preserving map.
That is, RSA can show that two spaces have similar geometry, but it does not identify the full mapping of one structure onto the other.
The Qualia Structure approach, discussed next, aims to take this next step (Tsuchiya 2025).

We will thus just briefly mention that this approach goes beyond traditional RSA by studying structural mappings between qualia structures, between neuronal information structures, as well as between qualia structures and neuronal information structures (Phillips and Tsuchiya 2024) (Figure 4).

text.text: A major shift in the study of spiking activity that differentiates the time period of the pioneering work on state-based and function-based NCC is that action potentials now routinely get measured across more than one neuron, or just a small number of neurons.
Instead, most direct measures of neuronal responses now comprise hundreds (and sometimes thousands) of neurons that were measured at the same time (Stringer et al. 2019).

text.text: For the purpose of this review, it will suffice to mention that IIT (in its current iteration, IIT4.0) seems unique among current theories.

That is, IIT is first and largely unrivaled in offering an explicit mathematical formalism that attempts to identify the structure of conscious experience with an information structure derived from physical (brain) mechanisms (Seth and Bayne 2022).

text.text: Most of the early work we discussed focused on "neuronal activation" (i.e., action potentials), with little regard to connectivity.
Recent work increasingly acknowledges that neuronal mechanisms comprise more than action potentials devoid of connective context (Gidon et al. 2022).
text.formatted: Recent work increasingly acknowledges that neuronal mechanisms comprise more than action potentials devoid of connective context <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Gidon et al. 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, there are many open questions regarding "connectivity".

Recent work in C. elegans suggests that the anatomical connections between neurons do not provide a valid prediction of the functional connectivity (Cook et al. 2019; Ripoll-Sánchez et al. 2023) between these neurons (i.e., which neurons tend to co-vary) (Uzel et al. 2022).
text.formatted: Recent work in C. elegans suggests that the anatomical connections between neurons do not provide a valid prediction of the functional connectivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Cook et al. 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">Ripoll-Sánchez et al. 2023)</ref> between these neurons (i.e., which neurons tend to co-vary) <ref type="bibr" target="#b173">(Uzel et al. 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, functional connectivity does not fully predict the effective connectivity of the same neurons (i.e., the causal effectiveness with which these neurons affect each other).
More than that, functional connectivity dynamically changes over time (Flavell and Gordus 2022).
text.formatted: More than that, functional connectivity dynamically changes over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Flavell and Gordus 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Mathematical mappings between brain mechanisms and conscious experience that consider both the activation state of neurons as well as their connectivity (and thus causal potentiality) thus face empirical challenges that we are only beginning to understand.
We then discussed a parallel approach in the pioneering literature that aimed to relate psychometric functions to neurometric functions.
Rightmost Column: Lastly, we discussed more recent approaches aimed at uncovering structure-preserving maps (e.g., homomorphisms) between neuronal mechanisms and conscious experiences.
Each of these approaches enjoys empirical success and they are not mutually exclusive.

Yet, arguably, there is an increased "richness" when moving from left to right in that correlations are commonly reduced to single number values (e.g., Pearson's r), two-dimensional functions can be related via two-dimensional correspondences, while high-dimensional structures might require higher-dimensional mappings.

The early neuroscience of consciousness largely focused on non-structural mathematical relations between brain mechanisms and conscious experiences, such as correlation coefficients and neurometric functions (Figure 4).

BOX 1: Glossary action potential (or spike): A brief (~1ms) electrical pulse by which a neuron transmits information to other neurons. binocular rivalry: A bistable stimulus in which each eye sees a different image, causing conscious perception to alternate. bistable (or multistable) stimulus: A stimulus that can lead to two or more different conscious experiences even though the physical input stays the same (e.g., binocular rivalry).
Often used in contrastive analysis.
The blood-oxygen-level-dependent signal measured by fMRI.

It indirectly reflects neuronal population activity rather than individual spikes. brain area: A region of the brain defined by neuroanatomy, function, or connectivity (e.g., the visual cortex). brain mechanism: A causal effect that arises from the combination of neuronal connectivity and neuronal activity.
bridge law: A formal rule that links brain descriptions (e.g., neuronal population activity) to experience (qualia).

bridge locus: The theoretical "meeting point" where brain mechanisms link to consciousness. choice probability: A value (usually between 0 and 1) that quantifies how well neuronal activity predicts a subject's choice in a two-alternative forced choice task. consciousness (subjective experience): What it is like to be in a certain state, or having a quale, such as seeing red, feeling pain, or thinking a thought.
A method that compares brain activity when consciousness is present versus absent (or different), often using bistable stimuli or no-report paradigms.
downstream activity: Brain activity that follows the NCC, such as decision making, reporting, or motor planning.
EEG: Electroencephalography: a method that measures electrical signals at the scalp.
These signals are produced by large groups of neurons, which cannot be fully localized inside the brain.
EEG has high time resolution (milliseconds), but low spatial resolution (which neurons caused the signal remains largely hidden). graph theory: The branch of mathematics that studies graphs.
The faintest stimulus that can be detected.
A key concept in psychophysics and psychometric functions. mapping: A rule that links one domain to another.
In neuroscience, it can link stimuli to brain activity; in mathematics, it links abstract structures.
mathematics: The formal study of numbers, structures, and relations.
mind-body problem: The philosophical problem of how objective physical processes in the brain relate to consciousness and qualia.
naturalism: The view that everything that exists is part of one coherent system (the universe), in which all causes stem only from within that system.
Often associated with science.
nervous system: All neurons within a body taken together.

neuroanatomy: The study of the brain's physical structure, including brain areas, and connectivity. neurometric function: A curve showing how well neuronal activity predicts reported conscious experience; analogous to a psychometric function but based on neural data.
neuron: A nerve cell that communicates with other nerve cells using action potentials.
Neurons form causal networks through neuronal connectivity.
neuronal connectivity: The physical wiring between neurons or brain areas.

Forms the basis of the (effective) connectome. neuronal correlate of consciousness (NCC): A neural state, process, or mechanism whose activity systematically covaries with a conscious state or content.
In stronger formulations: the minimal neural substrate sufficient for that experience.
Often studied using contrastive analysis.
The combined activity of many neurons.
Most brain measurements (EEG, fMRI) reflect such combined activity rather than single spikes.

neuroscience: The scientific study of the brain and nervous system. no-report paradigms: Experiments that infer conscious experience without asking subjects to report it, reducing confounds from downstream activity.
representational similarity: A method that compares patterns of neuronal population activity to see whether they encode similar information.
science: A method of investigating reality that relies on empirical evidence, logical reasoning, and repeatable testing of ideas (hypotheses) against observation.
signal detection theory: A mathematical framework describing how decisions are made under uncertainty.
Used with psychometric functions and choice probability.
structure: A formalizable organized set of elements and relations.
A method that uses topology to find robust structure in complex data, including neuronal population activity.
topology: The mathematical study of properties that stay the same under continuous deformation (e.g., stretching, bending).
A task where a subject must choose between two options.
Common in psychophysics and signal detection theory.
upstream activity: Brain activity that occurs before, and influences, the NCC but does not itself constitute the conscious experience.

text.text: Top: Physical stimulation (Retinal Input) is kept unchanging over time.
In the case of binocular rivalry, one image (e.g., a photograph of a face) is shown to one eye while a different image (e.g., a photograph of a house) is shown to the other eye.
When facing such conflict between the two eyes and if the stimuli are kept relatively small (1-2 degrees of visual angle), visual perception randomly alternates (switches) between each eye's view.

As a result, truthful subjects report that they either perceive one or the other image for brief periods of time (i.e., the Reported Percept alternates between the two mutually exclusive alternatives).

Middle: Some cortical neurons have been shown to either increase or decrease in firing rate whenever subjects report seeing one or the other image (i.e., researchers have found Single Neuron Activity that correlates with conscious perception).
Bottom left: Calculating the frequency of single neuron spiking during each of the two alternating perceptual states can be interpreted as two conditional probability distributions.
Bottom right: A statistical comparison of the mean or median spiking of a neuron to each of the two conscious perceptual states demonstrates significant differences in neuronal activation.

Any statistically significant difference in activation that occurs with alternating conscious experiences -despite constant retinal stimulation -is interpreted as a neuronal correlate of consciousness (NCC), suggesting that such a neuron's activity is associated with that conscious state.
